options: Actual business users who will use the system after go-live
questions.explain: UAT is run by actual business users — the people who will use the system daily after go-live — rather than the project team that ran SIT.

questions.q: Why does a strong UAT include business users' own real scenarios, not just adapted SIT scripts?
options: Because a consultant-written script can miss edge cases obvious only to someone who lives in the process daily
Because SIT scripts are always wrong
Because real scenarios are required by Oracle Support policy
Because UAT cannot reuse SIT scripts under any circumstance
questions.explain: Business users running their own real scenarios surface edge cases and patterns that a consultant's scripted test might never have anticipated.

questions.q: What does a formal UAT sign-off actually certify?
options: That the system has zero defects of any kind
That the Requirements Traceability Matrix is no longer needed
That the system meets the business's acceptance criteria and is ready to run on, even with some minor defects open
questions.explain: UAT sign-off certifies the system is ready for the business to run on — not that it is defect-free, since lower-severity defects can remain open with an agreed plan.

questions.q: UAT sign-off serves as the exit criterion for which TCM phase?
questions.explain: UAT sign-off is the exit criterion for TCM's Validate phase and the entry criterion for Transition, the phase gate concept introduced in Lesson 3.

questions.q: What new defect did Brightfield's Treasury Manager surface during UAT that SIT had not covered?
options: A foreign-currency wire transfer scenario needing special handling
questions.explain: The Treasury Manager's UAT testing surfaced a foreign-currency wire transfer scenario the SIT script had never covered, which became a new logged defect.
